name: Krache
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress
sweep_summary: Krache (krac1238) is not in the catalog. The sweep's single title hit, Kandybowicz & Torrence 2015 (ACAL 44, pp. 146-157; open PDF already on file), is about phrase-level prosody (L% boundary tones marking Phonological/Intonational Phrase right edges, pauses, pitch reset) as a licensing condition on wh-in-situ; it says nothing about word stress and describes Krachi as having two surface level tones (H, L) after Snider 1990. Five further Krachi texts already on file from the earlier pass (Abunya 2018 PhD grammar; Torrence & Kandybowicz 2015 JALL MS; two further Kandybowicz/Torrence MSS; Abunya & Osam 2022) were re-grepped: no word-stress statement anywhere; Abunya 2018 p.33 gives only 'Kaakye is a tonal language with two basic level tones: high and low (Snider 1990a)'. Snider 1990 (Language 66:453-474, doi 10.2307/414608) is paywalled; its abstract (read on Cambridge Core, saved as a note) concerns tonal upstep only. Adonae 2005 'Kaakyi Tonology' (MPhil, Legon; Glottolog 546832) is not online (UGSpace search empty) and is the only candidate that might contain an explicit stress/accent statement -- medium acquisition priority. Net: no first-hand stress statement exists in the reachable literature; Krachi is documented as a two-level register-tone language with boundary tones, and no catalog record is affected. sources.citation: Kandybowicz, Jason & Harold Torrence. 2015. The prosodic licensing of wh-in-situ: Evidence from Krachi and Wasa. In Ruth Kramer et al. (eds.), Selected Proceedings of the 44th Annual Conference on African Linguistics, 146-157. Somerville, MA: Cascadilla Proceedings Project.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: not located online or at Harvard
sources.quote: we use IPA to write our Krachi examples, using accent diacritics to represent Krachi's two surface level tones (Snider 1990). The acute accent is used to mark High tones. Low tones are unmarked. [p.147 fn.1] ... The right edges of phrasal prosodic constituents in Krachi are tonally marked and detectable via a number of salient phonetic cues. Kandybowicz and Torrence (2012a) show that Phonological Phrases in the language are right edge-marked by way of Low boundary tones (L%). In the same way, the right boundaries of Intonational Phrases in the language are marked by L%. [p.151]
sources.note: Nothing. The paper is about phrase-level prosodic phrasing (Intonational Phrase boundaries marked by L% boundary tones, pauses, pitch reset) as a licensing condition on wh-in-situ. It treats Krachi as a two-level-tone language (H, L) and the word 'stress' does not occur anywhere in the text.

sources.citation: Abunya, Levina Nyameye. 2018. Aspects of Kaakye Grammar. PhD thesis, University of Ghana, Legon. 378 pp. (handle 123456789/30309)
sources.quote: Kaakye is a tonal language with two basic level tones: high (´) and low (`), (Snider 1990a).
sources.note: Only a one-line tone statement; a grep of the whole 378-page text finds 'stress' only in 'stress-free environment' (fieldwork methods). No word-stress statement.

sources.citation: Torrence, Harold & Jason Kandybowicz. 2015. Wh-question formation in Krachi. Journal of African Languages and Linguistics 36(2). doi:10.1515/jall-2015-0011 (author MS, lingbuzz 006909)
sources.quote: Because the orthography does not mark Krachi's two surface level tones (High and Low (Snider 1990, Adonae 2005)), we have omitted tone marking from our representations.
sources.note: Nothing on stress; syntax paper, tone note only. Names Adonae 2005 as the other tonology source.

sources.citation: Kandybowicz, Jason & Harold Torrence. Krachi wh-in-situ: A question of prosody. WCCFL proceedings paper (author MS, lingbuzz 006906), 10 pp.
sources.quote: Krachi has three register tones (High, Mid, Low) as well as contour tones. In this article, High tones are indicated by means of acute accents, while Low tones are marked with grave accents. Mid tones are unmarked.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Note the discrepancy with the other papers (three register tones here vs two surface level tones elsewhere).

sources.citation: Kandybowicz, Jason. On prosodic variation and the distribution of wh-in-situ (Krachi, Bono, Wasa, Asante Twi). Author MS, lingbuzz 006905, 38 pp. (Linguistic Variation)
sources.quote: acute accents denote High tones; grave + acute accent sequences (e.g. ˇ) denote Rising tones; and acute + grave accent sequences (e.g. ˆ) denote Falling tones. Low tones are unmarked.
sources.note: Nothing on stress; only tone-diacritic conventions and Intonational-Phrase phrasing.

sources.quote: While descriptions and analyses of tonal downstep abound, considerably less attention has been devoted to cases involving tonal upstep ... I argue that the Krachi data are best analyzed as involving an upward shifting of the tonal register (upstep).
sources.note: Primary published tonal analysis of Krachi by the SIL/GILLBT fieldworker; its language-background section is the authoritative statement of the prosodic type (two tones + upstep) and may explicitly address stress/accent.
